attacks.claim: Rollback re-enables MailPoet but only re-imports new Ghost signups. Unsubscribes, bounces, complaints and paid-member changes (cancellations, plan changes) made in Ghost/Stripe after cutover are not synced back, so rollback could re-mail opted-out people and leave member state inconsistent. The reverse sync is manual, untested, unowned and untimed.
attacks.evidence: "rollback = repoint DNS and re-enable MailPoet sending, with any new Ghost signups exported and re-imported to MailPoet."

attacks.claim: The plan's purpose is ending send-day outages, but Ghost, MySQL and the send pipeline all stay on one VPS. No load test of a full 46k send concurrent with web traffic is planned, and there is no mid-send failure runbook, RTO/RPO, tested restore time, or monitoring and alerting for sends, backups or Stripe webhooks. The same single-box failure domain remains.
attacks.evidence: "MySQL 8 on the same box, nightly encrypted dumps to object storage (30-day retention)"; ABSENT: load test of a 46k-recipient send, monitoring/alerting, RTO/RPO

attacks.claim: The remainder of the list (~44k) sends automatically after the 2,000 seed if thresholds pass, with no named human go/no-go owner or abort step. Sent email cannot be recalled. Thresholds on a 2,000 seed are noisy (2 complaints trips 0.1%), the plan does not say what happens if the gate fails, and the warm-up is only about a week with no volume ramp.
attacks.evidence: "the remainder sends 2 hours later if bounce rate < 2% and complaint rate < 0.1%"; "Mailgun domain warm-up (SPF/DKIM/DMARC)"

attacks.claim: There is no pre-import snapshot or tested revert for the production import of 46k subscribers and 3,100 members. The 30-day WordPress window ends with no decommission gate or point-of-no-return definition, and no plan covers purging legacy member copies in MailPoet and the plugins.
attacks.evidence: "Dry-run import on staging in week 1; counts reconciled ... before the production import."; "WordPress stays running read-only on the old VPS for 30 days"

attacks.claim: The exit path, the plan's stated ownership guarantee, is rehearsed only with 50 addresses through Postmark. Postmark has no account, warm-up or DNS setup in the timeline. Throughput, suppression and consent survival, and the Mailgun feedback loop into Ghost at 46k scale are unverified, so a fallback would start cold at full volume.
attacks.evidence: "rehearse this end to end with a 50-address internal list through Postmark Broadcasts"; Week 2 list includes only "Mailgun domain warm-up"

attacks.claim: The cost claim against the $300 cap is weakly supported. Mailgun's $90/mo is an unsourced estimate, and the $140 total does not reconcile ($48 + $90 = $138, leaving ~$2 for storage). Overlap costs (old VPS for 30 days, staging, Postmark) are not counted.
attacks.evidence: "Estimated $90/mo at our volume (46k x ~4.3 sends/month)." / "Total run cost: ~$140/mo VPS + Mailgun + storage"

attacks.claim: There is no plan for secrets custody (Stripe and Mailgun keys, SMTP credentials, backup encryption key) or for Ghost admin access controls (MFA, staff roles, integration scoping). The old WordPress host stays online for 30 days with no stated enforcement of read-only or patching. These systems hold the full member list.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: secret storage, key custody/rotation, admin MFA/roles; "WordPress stays running read-only on the old VPS for 30 days"

attacks.claim: Personal data handling is incomplete. Weekly exports have no retention limit, staging and scratch instances get real subscriber data with no access or deletion rules, there is no erasure path covering backups, exports and legacy copies, and there are no processor agreements or reader notice for Mailgun, Postmark and the storage provider. The 37 hand-resolved member matches have no verification step.
attacks.evidence: "scheduled weekly (cron, stored with the DB dumps)" vs "30-day retention"; "37 members with mismatched emails ... resolved by hand"; ABSENT: DPA, erasure procedure

attacks.claim: Cutover-critical items are unaddressed. Media files are not covered by the DB dumps or JSON export. Stripe webhook movement, plugin deactivation without double-processing, and price/tier mapping are not covered. Unsubscribe links in already-sent MailPoet emails may break once WordPress goes read-only, a legal and deliverability risk. Paying members get no continuity or communication plan.
attacks.evidence: "Stripe: existing Stripe account connected directly; no change in processor."; "WordPress stays running read-only"; ABSENT: media backup, legacy unsubscribe handling, member communication

attacks.claim: The timeline is ambiguous about dates: the 'final Thursday send on MailPoet' in week 3 and the 'cutover Tuesday' in week 4 are not mapped to calendar dates. The 4-week scope (VPS, theme port, migrations, Stripe, Mailgun, training) rests on one 0.5 FTE developer with no backup and no feasibility check.
attacks.evidence: "Cutover target: Tuesday after week 3 send"; "Owner: dev (0.5 FTE) + managing editor | 4 weeks"
